# adr-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** MADR — Markdown Architectural Decision Records (template and guidance) — https://adr.github.io/madr/
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: an ADR is written from the decision itself, as made with the user against the codebase at hand; it consumes no other skill's output. The recorded decisions feed stack-selection, system-design, and decision-logs.
- **Feeds into:** stack-selection, system-design, decision-logs

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a significant, hard-to-reverse decision is being made — stack components, tenancy model, API paradigm, pattern adoption, data ownership — or an existing decision is being revisited or reversed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the choice is trivially reversible or purely local (a variable name, a file layout inside one module); record those in code review and move on. Do not use an ADR as the design document itself — the design lives in ARCHITECTURE.md or the contract, and the ADR links to it.

## Rules

1. **AR-241 — One file per decision.** Each record is its own MADR file in `docs/decisions/`, numbered `NNNN-title.md`; a file deciding two questions is split.
2. **AR-242 — Full MADR sections.** Every record carries: title, status, context and problem statement, decision drivers, considered options, decision outcome, and consequences.
3. **AR-243 — At least two considered options.** The rejected alternative and the reason it lost are mandatory. An ADR with one option is incomplete: the rejected option is the record's most valuable content.
4. **AR-244 — At least one negative consequence.** Consequences include at least one negative or cost. An all-positive consequences section means the trade-off was not examined, and the record is sent back.
5. **AR-245 — Immutable once accepted.** An accepted ADR is never edited to change its decision. A change of mind is a new ADR that supersedes the old one, linked in both directions.
6. **AR-246 — Status is maintained.** When a decision is reversed, the old record's status becomes "superseded by NNNN" in the same commit as the new ADR. The folder never holds two contradictory "accepted" records on the same question.
7. **AR-247 — Titles state the decision.** The title is the decision in a sentence — "Use PostgreSQL for the primary store" — not the topic, "Database discussion."
8. **AR-248 — Written with the work.** The ADR lands in the same change as the work it governs, while the alternatives are still genuinely remembered, not reconstructed weeks later.
9. **AR-249 — Decisions, not designs.** The ADR records the choice and its reasoning; the full design lives in ARCHITECTURE.md or the contract, and the ADR links to it instead of copying it.
10. **AR-250 — Every significant decision gets one.** If reversing the choice would cost more than a day's work, it needs an ADR: stack components, tenancy model, paradigm, pattern adoptions, data ownership.
11. **AR-251 — Drivers before options.** Decision drivers and selection criteria are recorded before options are scored against them; criteria written after the winner is known are rationalization.
12. **AR-252 — Links resolve.** Supersedes and superseded-by links, and every referenced diagram, contract, and ADR, point at files that exist.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-121 — The silent swap.** Banned: changing a settled, ADR-backed decision with no new ADR recording the change. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: write the superseding ADR with the new decision's drivers and rejected alternatives, and update the old record's status in the same commit. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-122 — Editing history.** Banned: modifying an accepted ADR's decision, options, or consequences in place. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: leave the record untouched; write a new ADR that supersedes it and states what changed. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-123 — The all-positive record.** Banned: a consequences section listing only benefits. Defeats: DET-CODE-021. Instead: name at least one real cost (operational burden, lock-in, a capability given up) and who bears it. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-124 — Topic titles.** Banned: titling an ADR with its subject area instead of its decision. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: `0007-use-postgresql-for-the-primary-store.md`. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-121 — ADR lint.** Verifies: AR-242, AR-243, AR-245, AR-252. Check: automated — a script over `docs/decisions/` asserts every file parses, carries a status from the allowed set (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded by NNNN), has a considered-options section with at least two options, and that superseded records link to an existing successor. Pass: zero violations. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-122 — Manifest cross-check.** Verifies: AR-250. Check: automated — every top-level dependency in the project's manifest maps to an ADR (by name or tag match). Pass: every major dependency has a record. Fail: block the dependency addition until its ADR exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-123 — Reconstruction test.** Verifies: AR-243, AR-244. Check: manual — sample one ADR and confirm a reader who was not present can reconstruct why the choice was made, including what was given up, without interviewing the author. Pass: the reader's summary matches the decision's actual drivers. Fail: warn; the record is expanded before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-124 — Contradiction scan.** Verifies: AR-246. Check: manual — at each release, scan the accepted ADRs for two records deciding the same question differently. Pass: no contradictory pair marked accepted. Fail: block release until one is superseded. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- One file, one decision, at least two options.
- The rejected alternative is the most valuable part.
- Every record names a cost.
- Accepted records are immutable; reversal means a new ADR.
- The title is the decision, not the topic.

## Checklist

- [ ] The record is one MADR file, titled with the decision (AR-241, AR-247).
- [ ] Considered options number at least two, with the loser's reason stated (AR-243).
- [ ] Consequences include at least one negative or cost (AR-244).
- [ ] Decision drivers were recorded before options were scored (AR-251).
- [ ] ADR lint passes over `docs/decisions/` (G-AR-121).
- [ ] If this reverses a decision, the old record's status is updated in the same commit (AR-246).
- [ ] The ADR links to the design instead of copying it, and all links resolve (AR-249, AR-252).

# api-architecture

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Zalando RESTful API Guidelines — https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/ ; Google API design and compatibility rules — https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/compatibility/ ; Lint and diff tooling survey — https://apidog.com/blog/open-source-cli-tools-api-design/
- **Depends on:** system-design, domain-driven-design
- **Feeds into:** api-versioning, api-documentation, api-paradigms

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing a new HTTP API or a new resource surface on an existing one; reviewing an OpenAPI draft before implementation; settling naming, error, pagination, or idempotency conventions for a service.
- **Do NOT use when:** the interface is not resource-oriented HTTP (api-paradigms decides the paradigm first), the question is only how an accepted design evolves (api-versioning), or the work is documenting an existing contract (api-documentation).

**House profile (applies to this skill, api-versioning, and api-documentation — one style, no mixing):** Zalando-based. Resource names are plural nouns; property names are `snake_case`; custom actions are sub-resources (e.g., `POST /orders/{id}/cancellations`); errors use the Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) everywhere; collections paginate with cursors; the major version sits in the path segment (`/v1/…`); deprecations are signaled with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers.

## Rules

1. **AR-061 — Contract first.** The OpenAPI document is drafted and reviewed before implementation, and is written or updated in the same change as any API behavior change. Code that changes behavior without touching the contract is incomplete.
2. **AR-062 — Resources from the domain.** Resources and their relationships are identified from the domain model, with stable identifiers. An endpoint that cannot name its resource is a design smell to resolve, not to route around.
3. **AR-063 — One error format.** Every endpoint returns errors in the house Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`). Per-endpoint error shapes are a blocking defect.
4. **AR-064 — Every list paginates.** Every list endpoint paginates (cursor preferred) and states its ordering in the contract. An unbounded list response is forbidden.
5. **AR-065 — Filtering and sorting are first-version features.** Collection endpoints define their filter and sort parameters in the first version, per the house profile; bolting them on later is a breaking-change risk, not a plan.
6. **AR-066 — Mutations state their idempotency story.** Every mutating endpoint is one of: a safe/idempotent method by semantics, protected by an idempotency key, or explicitly documented as non-idempotent with a retry warning. Silence on idempotency is a defect.
7. **AR-067 — Names follow the house profile.** Resource names are plural nouns; verbs appear only as named sub-resource actions (`/orders/{id}/cancellations`); property names are `snake_case`. No endpoint invents its own convention.
8. **AR-068 — Auth is in the contract.** Every operation declares its security requirement in the OpenAPI document (scheme and, where applicable, scope). An operation with no declared security is treated as an oversight, not as public-by-default.
9. **AR-069 — One profile, applied uniformly.** The house profile named in this skill is the only style guide for the API. Where the profile is silent, the gap is resolved once, recorded, and applied everywhere — never per endpoint.
10. **AR-070 — Breaking changes leave this skill.** Any change the compatibility list classifies as breaking is routed to api-versioning (major bump plus deprecation window); it never ships quietly inside an existing version.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-031 — Per-endpoint error shapes.** Banned: each endpoint inventing its own error body. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: the house Problem Details body (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) from every endpoint (AR-063). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-032 — The unbounded list.** Banned: a list endpoint that returns the whole collection. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: cursor pagination with a stated ordering and a default and maximum page size, in the first version (AR-064). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-033 — Verbs as resources.** Banned: endpoints named for actions instead of resources (`/createOrder`, `/getInvoices`, `/deleteUser`). Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: plural-noun resources with HTTP methods for the standard operations and sub-resource actions for the rest (`POST /orders`, `POST /orders/{id}/cancellations`) (AR-067). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-034 — Code-first drift.** Banned: shipping an API behavior change while the OpenAPI document stays untouched. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: the contract is edited in the same change, reviewed as the contract, and the diff gate in api-versioning classifies the rename as breaking (AR-061). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-031 — OpenAPI lint.** Verifies: AR-063, AR-064, AR-067, AR-068. Check: automated — CI runs Spectral (or Redocly CLI) with the house ruleset against the OpenAPI file: operationIds and descriptions present, error responses use the Problem Details schema, list operations declare pagination parameters, property names match `snake_case`. The linter version is pinned in the repo; if the sandbox cannot run it, the fallback is the documented manual ruleset walk, recorded in progress.md. Pass: zero lint errors. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-032 — Contract tests.** Verifies: AR-061, AR-063. Check: automated — contract tests generated from the OpenAPI document run against the implementation in CI and assert status codes, response shapes, and the error format on failure paths. Pass: all contract tests green. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-033 — Spec-diff design review.** Verifies: AR-062, AR-066, AR-069. Check: manual — before implementation starts, a reviewer reads the OpenAPI diff: resources trace to the domain model, every mutation states its idempotency story, and every deviation from the house profile is recorded as a profile decision. Pass: no unresolved findings. Fail: block implementation. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Contract first, code second — same change, every time.
- One error format: Problem Details, everywhere.
- Every list paginates; every mutation states its idempotency story.
- Plural nouns, snake_case, sub-resource actions — the house profile.
- Breaking change? Stop — api-versioning owns it.

## Checklist

- [ ] The OpenAPI document was drafted or updated in the same change as the behavior (AR-061).
- [ ] OpenAPI lint passes with the house ruleset (G-AR-031).
- [ ] Contract tests run against the implementation and pass (G-AR-032).
- [ ] Every error response uses the Problem Details format (AR-063).
- [ ] Every list endpoint paginates with a stated ordering (AR-064).
- [ ] Every mutating endpoint states its idempotency story (AR-066).
- [ ] Every operation declares its security requirement (AR-068).
- [ ] Names follow the house profile with no per-endpoint exceptions (AR-067, AR-069).

# api-documentation

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 ; Redocly CLI lint and bundle in the docs pipeline (tooling survey) — https://apidog.com/blog/open-source-cli-tools-api-design/
- **Depends on:** api-architecture, api-versioning
- **Feeds into:** api-versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** producing or repairing an API's reference documentation; setting up docs generation from the OpenAPI document; auditing published docs against the running API.
- **Do NOT use when:** the contract itself is still being designed (api-architecture) or does not exist — documentation cannot be generated from a contract that was never written. Do not use this skill to hand-write a reference that duplicates the spec.

**House profile (shared with api-architecture and api-versioning):** the reference is generated from the OpenAPI document; errors are documented in the shared Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`); property names in examples are `snake_case`; each version's docs publish under its own path segment and stay reachable for the version's whole lifetime.

## Rules

1. **AR-101 — Generated, never hand-maintained.** The reference documentation is generated from the OpenAPI document. Paths, schemas, and status codes are never edited by hand in a parallel document.
2. **AR-102 — The spec is the boundary.** If it is not in the OpenAPI document, it is not documented; if it is in the document, it renders in the reference. Side wikis are never the source of truth.
3. **AR-103 — Errors are documented for every endpoint.** Every operation documents its error responses in the shared Problem Details format. A "TODO: document errors" note shipped as final is a blocking defect.
4. **AR-104 — Examples are real and executed.** Examples are real requests with realistic, non-sensitive data, and every example payload is verified by executing it against a running instance — fields, types, and required values accepted by the real API, not checked by eye.
5. **AR-105 — Authentication is a complete flow.** Auth is documented as a walkthrough: obtain the credential, send it, its expiry and refresh behavior, and the failure response. "Use your API key" is not documentation.
6. **AR-106 — Humans write only the layer generation cannot.** Human-written docs are limited to the authentication walkthrough, one runnable example per endpoint group, the error catalog, and the changelog. Everything else is generated.
7. **AR-107 — Docs version with the API.** Documentation publishes with the API version it describes, under that version's path; older versions' docs stay reachable for the whole deprecation window defined by api-versioning.
8. **AR-108 — Changelog in the same change.** Each release updates the docs changelog in the same change as the contract change. A contract change without its changelog entry is incomplete.
9. **AR-109 — No sensitive data in examples.** Example payloads never contain real credentials, tokens, personal data, or production identifiers — realistic shape, synthetic values.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-051 — "TODO: document errors" shipped as final.** Banned: publishing documentation with error sections left as TODOs or omitted. Defeats: DET-CODE-011. Instead: every operation documents its Problem Details error responses before the docs publish (AR-103). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-052 — The parallel hand-written wiki.** Banned: a hand-maintained wiki or doc page that restates paths, fields, or status codes from the spec. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Instead: generate the reference from the OpenAPI document and delete the restated pages, keeping only the human layer (AR-101, AR-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-053 — The example the API rejects.** Banned: an example payload the real API would refuse — wrong field names, wrong types, missing required values. Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Instead: execute every example against a running instance in CI and fix the example or the API until it passes (AR-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-054 — Documented endpoints that do not exist.** Banned: reference entries for endpoints the service does not route. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: the docs are generated from the shipped spec and the example-execution gate proves every documented path responds (AR-102, AR-104). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-051 — Example execution.** Verifies: AR-104, AR-109. Check: automated — CI executes every documented example request (at minimum three per endpoint group, all of them where the suite is small) against a staging instance and asserts the documented status code and response shape. Pass: every executed example matches its documentation. Fail: block docs publication. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-052 — Documentation lint.** Verifies: AR-102, AR-103, AR-105. Check: automated — Spectral/Redocly rules over the OpenAPI document require a description and at least one example on every operation, a Problem Details error response on every operation, and a declared security scheme; the string "TODO" anywhere in the document fails the build. Pass: zero lint errors. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-053 — Docs-to-routes diff.** Verifies: AR-101, AR-102. Check: automated — a script compares the paths in the published OpenAPI document against the running service's route table. Pass: zero documented-but-unrouted paths and zero routed-but-undocumented public paths. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Generated from the spec — never hand-maintained in parallel.
- Not in the OpenAPI document? Not documented.
- Every example is executed, not eyeballed.
- Errors are documented for every endpoint, in Problem Details.
- Docs version with the API; old versions stay reachable.

## Checklist

- [ ] The reference is generated from the current OpenAPI document (AR-101).
- [ ] Every operation documents its error responses; no TODOs remain (G-AR-052).
- [ ] Every documented example executes successfully against a running instance (G-AR-051).
- [ ] Authentication is documented as a complete flow, including failure (AR-105).
- [ ] The docs-to-routes diff shows zero mismatches (G-AR-053).
- [ ] The changelog entry landed in the same change as the contract (AR-108).
- [ ] Examples contain synthetic values only — no real credentials or personal data (AR-109).

# api-paradigms

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** GraphQL Specification, October 2021 edition — https://spec.graphql.org/October2021/ ; OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 ; AsyncAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.1.0
- **Depends on:** api-architecture, system-design
- **Feeds into:** event-driven, api-documentation

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** choosing the interface paradigm for a new surface (REST, GraphQL, gRPC, event-based, end-to-end-typed RPC), or reviewing whether an existing surface is on the wrong paradigm.
- **Do NOT use when:** the paradigm is already settled and the work is designing within it (api-architecture for REST), or the question is how events themselves are specified once an event-based interface is chosen (event-driven).

## Rules

1. **AR-121 — The choice is an ADR naming the interaction shape.** Every paradigm adoption is recorded in an ADR that names the interaction shape driving it: resource CRUD, client-shaped reads, streaming, or fan-out facts. A paradigm with no stated shape has no justification.
2. **AR-122 — REST is the default.** REST over HTTP+JSON is the default for resource CRUD and for all public APIs. Any other paradigm carries the burden of proof in its ADR.
3. **AR-123 — GraphQL must earn its place.** GraphQL is adopted only when multiple client types need divergent, client-shaped reads over a richly connected graph — and the ADR names those clients and the reads.
4. **AR-124 — GraphQL ships with cost controls.** A GraphQL API ships with query depth and complexity limits and a field deprecation policy (`@deprecated` in the schema). An unbounded public GraphQL endpoint is a defect.
5. **AR-125 — gRPC stays internal by default.** gRPC fits internal service-to-service calls needing strict contracts and streaming performance. Exposing gRPC to public consumers requires an explicit ADR overruling this default.
6. **AR-126 — Events are for facts with independent consumers.** An event-based interface is chosen when multiple consumers react independently to facts. If one producer secretly depends on one specific consumer executing, it is a command, not an event — model it as one.
7. **AR-127 — Typed RPC stays inside one codebase.** tRPC-style end-to-end-typed RPC is acceptable only inside a single TypeScript codebase with no external consumers. The moment an outside client appears, a contract-first paradigm replaces it.
8. **AR-128 — No paradigm hides a modeling problem.** If the resources cannot be named, no paradigm fixes it. Unnameable resources send the work back to domain modeling, not to a more flexible query language.
9. **AR-129 — Every paradigm has its contract artifact.** Each paradigm in use keeps its contract in the repo: OpenAPI for REST, the SDL for GraphQL, `.proto` for gRPC, AsyncAPI for events. No contract artifact, no interface.
10. **AR-130 — Public surfaces get the boring paradigm.** Public consumers get the most boring paradigm that fits (REST first). Internal novelty never leaks into the public surface.
11. **AR-131 — Mixed paradigms are justified per surface.** Mixing paradigms is allowed; each surface's choice is justified by its own interaction shape in its own ADR. One paradigm's justification never covers another surface by association.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-061 — The unbounded public GraphQL endpoint.** Banned: exposing GraphQL publicly with no query depth or complexity limits. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: ship depth and complexity limits, and persisted queries where clients are known, before the endpoint is public (AR-124). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-062 — Paradigm by fashion.** Banned: adopting a paradigm with no ADR and no named interaction shape. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Instead: write the ADR naming the interaction shape, or take the REST default (AR-121, AR-122). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-063 — The contractless interface.** Banned: an interface in production with no contract artifact in the repo. Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Instead: commit the contract artifact — OpenAPI, SDL, `.proto`, or AsyncAPI — as the interface's source of truth (AR-129). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-064 — Flexibility as a modeling shortcut.** Banned: choosing GraphQL or generic RPC to avoid naming the domain's resources. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: return to domain modeling until the resources can be named, then pick the paradigm (AR-128). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-061 — Contract artifact validation.** Verifies: AR-129. Check: automated — CI validates whichever artifacts exist: OpenAPI lint for REST, GraphQL SDL validation against the spec's type-system rules, `protoc` compilation for gRPC, AsyncAPI validation for events. Pass: every artifact validates. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-062 — GraphQL limits check.** Verifies: AR-124. Check: automated — if a GraphQL schema exists, a script confirms the server configuration sets a maximum query depth and a complexity limit, and the schema's deprecations use `@deprecated`. Pass: both limits configured. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-063 — ADR-to-traffic review.** Verifies: AR-121, AR-123, AR-131. Check: manual — for each paradigm in use, read its ADR and compare the stated interaction shape with the API's actual dominant traffic (logs or analytics). Pass: every paradigm's stated shape matches its real traffic. Fail: warn and open a re-evaluation ADR. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Name the interaction shape, or take the REST default.
- GraphQL earns its place — and ships with cost controls.
- gRPC internal, events for facts, typed RPC inside one codebase.
- No contract artifact, no interface.
- Public consumers get the boring paradigm.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every paradigm in use has an ADR naming its interaction shape (AR-121).
- [ ] Public surfaces use REST unless an ADR proves another paradigm (AR-122, AR-130).
- [ ] GraphQL, where used, has depth/complexity limits and a deprecation policy (G-AR-062).
- [ ] Every interface has its contract artifact in the repo, validating in CI (G-AR-061).
- [ ] Event-based surfaces carry facts for independent consumers, not hidden commands (AR-126).
- [ ] Typed RPC, where used, has no external consumers (AR-127).
- [ ] Each mixed-paradigm surface is justified by its own ADR (AR-131).

# api-versioning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — https://semver.org/ ; Google, "Compatibility" (breaking vs non-breaking change lists) — https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/compatibility/ ; Breaking-change gate design — https://www.api-contract-testing.com/api-contract-fundamentals-tool-selection/breaking-change-detection/
- **Depends on:** api-architecture
- **Feeds into:** api-documentation

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an API change must be classified as breaking or safe; a major version is being introduced; a version is being deprecated or removed; a consumer asks what a version number promises.
- **Do NOT use when:** the API does not exist yet (api-architecture designs v1), or the version in question is a library/package version with no API consumers — though the same semver rules are a sound default there too.

**House profile (shared with api-architecture and api-documentation):** the major version sits in the path segment (`/v1/…`) and nowhere else; deprecations are signaled with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers plus a changelog entry; within a major version only backward-compatible changes ship.

## Rules

1. **AR-081 — Breaking is an enumerated list, not a feeling.** Removing or renaming a field, method, or enum value; changing a field's type; changing a resource name format; or changing visible behavior is breaking. Adding interfaces, methods, fields, or enum values is safe. The classification follows the list, never intuition.
2. **AR-082 — Unlisted means breaking.** A change the list does not cover is treated as breaking until a recorded ruling says otherwise. The benefit of the doubt goes to consumers.
3. **AR-083 — Additive only within a major version.** Inside a major version, only backward-compatible changes ship: additive fields, new endpoints, new enum values where consumers tolerate unknowns. Anything else waits for the next major.
4. **AR-084 — Breaking under the same major is release-blocking.** A breaking change that reaches a release under the existing major version is a release-blocking defect, however small it looks.
5. **AR-085 — Every version has a changelog.** Each version carries a changelog entry connecting the version to its changes. "Latest" is never the only nameable version of the API.
6. **AR-086 — Deprecation needs three artifacts first.** Before a deprecation window starts, all three exist: the sunset date, the migration path, and the consumer notification (docs plus `Deprecation`/`Sunset` headers). A window announced without them has not started.
7. **AR-087 — Removal waits for the date and the check.** The old version is removed only after the announced sunset date has passed and a consumer check shows no remaining traffic (or named consumers who accepted the cutoff in writing).
8. **AR-088 — Consumers must tolerate unknowns.** The contract states that consumers ignore unknown fields and enum values. This obligation is what makes additive changes safe, and it is written down, not assumed.
9. **AR-089 — One placement, never mixed.** The version identifier lives in the path segment for public HTTP APIs, per the house profile. Header-based and query-parameter versioning never appear in the same API.
10. **AR-090 — Old and new run side by side.** During a deprecation window both major versions are deployed and supported; a flag-day cutover, where the old version dies the moment the new one ships, is forbidden for public APIs.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-041 — The quiet breaking change.** Banned: shipping a breaking change under the same major version. Defeats: DET-INF-026. Instead: ship the rename in `/v2/`, run both side by side, and deprecate v1 with the full artifact set (AR-084, AR-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-042 — The random version bump.** Banned: version numbers bumped without a change classification behind them. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Instead: classify the change against the enumerated list first (AR-081); the bump follows the classification — patch for safe fixes, major for breaking changes. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-043 — The silent removal.** Banned: removing a deprecated version with no sunset date, no migration path, or no consumer notification. Defeats: DET-INF-028. Instead: publish the sunset date, the migration path, and the notification first; remove only after the date and the consumer check (AR-086, AR-087). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-044 — Mixed version placement.** Banned: version identifiers in more than one location in the same API. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: path segment only, per the house profile, for every endpoint (AR-089). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-041 — Breaking-change diff.** Verifies: AR-081, AR-083, AR-084. Check: automated — CI runs `oasdiff breaking <last-shipped-spec> <new-spec>`; any breaking finding fails the build unless the change also bumps the major version and lands with an ADR recording the approved break. The tool is pinned in the repo; if it cannot run in the sandbox, the fallback is a manual field-by-field diff against the compatibility list, recorded in progress.md. Pass: no unapproved breaking findings. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-042 — Deprecation artifact check.** Verifies: AR-086, AR-087. Check: automated — for any version marked deprecated, a script confirms the changelog contains its sunset date and migration link, and a probe of the running service confirms responses carry `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers. Pass: all three artifacts present. Fail: block the deprecation announcement. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-043 — Runtime version matches the tag.** Verifies: AR-085, AR-089. Check: automated — query the deployed service's metadata/health endpoint and compare its reported API version with the release tag and the path segments it serves. Pass: exact match. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Breaking is a list, not a feeling; unlisted means breaking.
- Additive only, inside a major version.
- Deprecation = sunset date + migration path + notification, before the window.
- Removal waits for the date and the consumer check.
- Path segment, one placement, never mixed.

## Checklist

- [ ] The change is classified against the enumerated compatibility list (AR-081).
- [ ] The breaking-change diff passes, or the break is approved with a major bump and an ADR (G-AR-041).
- [ ] The version has a changelog entry connecting it to its changes (AR-085).
- [ ] The contract states consumers must ignore unknown fields and enum values (AR-088).
- [ ] Any deprecation has its sunset date, migration path, and notification in place (G-AR-042).
- [ ] Old and new majors run side by side for the whole window (AR-090).
- [ ] The deployed version matches the release tag (G-AR-043).

# architecture-patterns

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microservices.io pattern language (Saga, CQRS, event sourcing, transactional outbox, database per service) — https://microservices.io/ ; Fowler, "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?" — https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html
- **Depends on:** system-design, adr-writing
- **Feeds into:** api-architecture, event-driven, domain-driven-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a distributed-systems or structural pattern (Saga, CQRS, event sourcing, transactional outbox, database per service, and their kin) is proposed for a project, or an existing design claims a pattern that needs auditing.
- **Do NOT use when:** the choice is a routine local design decision with no cross-component consequences — record it in code and move on. Do not use this skill to pick libraries or frameworks; that is stack-selection.

## Rules

1. **AR-161 — Named catalog only.** Patterns are selected from a named catalog (the microservices.io pattern language, Fowler's pattern writings) and cited by their catalog name; invented pattern names are not adopted.
2. **AR-162 — Problem before pattern.** No pattern is adopted without a stated problem it solves in this project. "For scale" without a load figure is not a problem statement.
3. **AR-163 — Four-part adoption record.** Before adoption, the ADR fills in all four parts from the catalog entry: the problem, the forces, the solution shape, and the consequences for this project.
4. **AR-164 — The hard part is the deliverable.** Adopting Saga requires named compensating transactions; CQRS requires the read-model synchronization design; event sourcing requires the event store and replay procedure. The label without the mechanism is not an adoption.
5. **AR-165 — No decorative infrastructure.** A queue or broker in the diagram while all interactions remain synchronous request/response is decoration and fails review.
6. **AR-166 — Consequences accepted in writing.** Every adoption records the consequences it accepts — eventual-consistency window, operational components added, new failure modes — in the ADR.
7. **AR-167 — Simplest variant first.** Prefer choreography before orchestration for short sagas and a single read model before multiple. The ADR records what measured change would trigger the complex variant.
8. **AR-168 — One pattern at a time.** Patterns are adopted incrementally, each behind its own ADR; a big-bang re-architecture introducing several at once is not approved.
9. **AR-169 — Default composition.** The default for a typical web application is a modular monolith with feature modules. A distributed composition must cite the requirement that forces it.
10. **AR-170 — Exit cost noted.** Every adoption records what removing or replacing the pattern would cost, so the decision can be revisited honestly.
11. **AR-171 — The mechanism must exist in code.** A pattern claimed in ARCHITECTURE.md must have its mechanism findable in the codebase — the outbox table, the compensating handlers, the read model. A claim without a mechanism is marked false.
12. **AR-172 — Module boundaries are enforced.** Modules and contexts expose public interfaces; cross-module imports of internals are forbidden and checked mechanically.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-081 — Pattern adopted "for scale".** Banned: adopting a distributed pattern with no stated problem and no load figure behind it. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Instead: state the problem the pattern solves here, with the number that proves it, or stay with the modular monolith. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-082 — Decorative broker.** Banned: installing a queue or broker while every interaction stays synchronous request/response. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: either adopt a named event pattern with its contract and consumers, or remove the broker and the claim. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-083 — Saga without compensations.** Banned: claiming the Saga pattern with no compensating transaction defined for each step. Defeats: DET-CODE-006. Instead: name and implement the compensation for every step before the saga ships; a step with no compensation is a step the saga may not take. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-084 — Reach-around imports.** Banned: one module importing another module's internal files, bypassing its public interface. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: consume the module's published interface, or propose the missing capability as part of that interface. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-081 — Pattern audit.** Verifies: AR-164, AR-171. Check: manual — for each pattern claimed in ARCHITECTURE.md, find its mechanism in code (outbox table, compensating handlers, read model) or mark the claim false. Pass: every claimed pattern has a mechanism. Fail: block release until the mechanism exists or the claim is removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-082 — Dependency-rule check.** Verifies: AR-172. Check: automated — CI lint rules forbid cross-module imports except through public interfaces. Pass: lint exits 0. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-083 — Adoption record completeness.** Verifies: AR-162, AR-163, AR-166, AR-170. Check: manual — each adopted pattern's ADR contains the problem with its evidence, the forces, the accepted consequences, and the exit cost. Pass: all four parts present for every adopted pattern. Fail: block adoption. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-084 — Simplicity review.** Verifies: AR-167, AR-169. Check: manual — for each adoption of Saga, CQRS, or event sourcing, confirm the ADR states why the simpler default was insufficient and what trigger would justify the complex variant. Pass: both statements present. Fail: warn; the adoption proceeds only with the trigger recorded. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Problem before pattern, always.
- The hard part is the deliverable, not the label.
- A broker with only synchronous calls is decoration.
- Simplest variant first; record the trigger for the complex one.
- If the mechanism is not in the code, the pattern is not in the system.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every adopted pattern is cited by its catalog name (AR-161).
- [ ] Every adoption's ADR states the problem, with the load figure or evidence behind it (AR-162).
- [ ] Compensations, read-model sync, or replay procedure are named for Saga, CQRS, or event sourcing adoptions (AR-164).
- [ ] Accepted consequences and exit cost are recorded per adoption (AR-166, AR-170).
- [ ] Pattern audit passed: every claimed pattern's mechanism found in code (G-AR-081).
- [ ] Dependency-rule lint exits 0 (G-AR-082).
- [ ] The simplest variant is in place, with the complex variant's trigger recorded (AR-167).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/c4-diagrams/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# c4-diagrams

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** C4 model, notation and diagram guidance — https://c4model.com/
- **Depends on:** system-design
- **Feeds into:** adr-writing, api-architecture

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** architecture needs to be communicated or reviewed — a new system context or container view, a container whose internals are non-obvious, or a diagram that has drifted from the system it describes.
- **Do NOT use when:** there is no architecture decision to communicate yet (system-design comes first), or the audience needs the API surface rather than the structure (api-documentation). Do not produce a Level 3 component diagram for a container whose internals are a standard framework layout.

## Rules

1. **AR-021 — Produce only the levels the audience needs.** Level 1 (system context) and Level 2 (containers) are the default set. Level 3 (components) is drawn only where a container's internal structure is non-obvious. Level 4 (code) is generated by tools or omitted.
2. **AR-022 — Every element is typed.** Each element is declared as a person, software system, container, or component, and each container states its technology. An untyped box is incomplete.
3. **AR-023 — Every relationship is labeled.** Each line carries the interaction and its protocol or format ("Places orders via HTTPS/JSON"). An unlabeled line fails review.
4. **AR-024 — Stores and queues are containers.** Data stores and queues appear as first-class containers in Level 2, never as annotations, footnotes, or icons attached to another box.
5. **AR-025 — Diagrams live as code.** Diagram sources (Structurizr DSL, PlantUML, or Mermaid) are kept in the repo and reviewed like code, so they diff in pull requests. A pasted image with no source in the repo is not a diagram of record.
6. **AR-026 — One view per diagram, with a legend.** Each diagram serves one audience and one level, and carries a legend for its element types. Two audiences are never merged into one picture.
7. **AR-027 — No generic labels.** Element names name the actual thing ("Orders API", "PostgreSQL — orders store"). "Frontend / Backend / Database" as the whole model is an automatic fail.
8. **AR-028 — External systems show direction and mode.** Every external system is drawn with the direction of each integration and whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.
9. **AR-029 — Diagrams change with the architecture.** A diagram is updated in the same change that alters the architecture it depicts, and the ADR for that change links the updated diagram. A diagram known to be stale is a defect, not a backlog item.
10. **AR-030 — Context shows people and systems only.** The Level 1 diagram shows the system as one box, its users, and the external systems it touches — no internal containers leak into the context view.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-011 — The all-in-one mega-diagram.** Banned: one picture mixing context, containers, components, and code-level classes for every audience at once. Defeats: DET-CODE-016. Instead: separate Level 1, 2, and (where earned) 3 diagrams, one view each, each with a legend (AR-021, AR-026). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-012 — Generic-label model.** Banned: a diagram whose elements are named only "Frontend", "Backend", "Database". Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: name each element for the real unit it represents, with its technology (AR-027). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-013 — The stale diagram.** Banned: leaving a diagram unchanged in a change that alters the architecture it depicts. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Instead: update the diagram source in the same pull request, and link it from the ADR (AR-029). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-014 — Image-only diagram.** Banned: a diagram that exists only as an exported PNG or a slide screenshot, with no source in the repo. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Instead: commit the Structurizr/PlantUML/Mermaid source and let the image be a build artifact (AR-025). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-011 — Diagram render check.** Verifies: AR-025. Check: automated — CI renders every diagram source with the pinned renderer (e.g., the project's locked Mermaid CLI or PlantUML jar) and fails on a non-zero exit; if the sandbox cannot run the renderer, the fallback is a manual render in the project's documented tool, recorded in progress.md. Pass: every source renders. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-012 — Label lint.** Verifies: AR-023, AR-027. Check: automated — grep the diagram sources for elements named exactly "Frontend", "Backend", or "Database" and for relationship lines with empty labels. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-013 — Element-to-deployment diff.** Verifies: AR-024, AR-028, AR-029. Check: manual — each release, diff the container diagram element by element against the deployment config: every deployable, store, and queue appears, and every external system shows direction and sync/async mode. Pass: zero differences. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Levels 1 and 2 by default; Level 3 only where it earns its keep.
- Typed elements, labeled lines, legend on every view.
- Stores and queues are containers, not decorations.
- Diagrams are code in the repo — they diff or they rot.
- Architecture changed? The diagram changes in the same pull request.

## Checklist

- [ ] Only the needed C4 levels exist, one view per diagram, each with a legend (AR-021, AR-026).
- [ ] Every element is typed and named for the real unit, with its technology (AR-022, AR-027).
- [ ] Every relationship line states the interaction and protocol (AR-023).
- [ ] Data stores and queues are first-class containers (AR-024).
- [ ] Diagram sources render cleanly in CI, or the manual fallback is recorded (G-AR-011).
- [ ] The release diff against the deployment config shows zero differences (G-AR-013).
- [ ] External systems show direction and sync/async mode (AR-028).

---

# data-architecture

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** MongoDB Manual, data modeling (embed vs reference by access pattern) — http://mongodocs.github.io/core/data-modeling-introduction.html ; Database-per-service and data ownership patterns — https://microservices.io/
- **Depends on:** system-design, requirements-writing
- **Feeds into:** schema-design, tenant-isolation, migrations

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project needs its data model designed or changed: choosing structures for a relational or document store, deciding embed vs reference, placing data ownership across services, or reviewing a schema before migrations are written.
- **Do NOT use when:** the model already exists and the task is writing or reviewing the migrations themselves — go to migrations and schema-design instead. Do not use this skill to tune individual queries in a settled schema; that is query-performance.

## Rules

1. **AR-141 — Access patterns first.** List the reads and writes each main screen and job performs before choosing any structure; a schema designed from nouns alone is sent back.
2. **AR-142 — Every entity maps.** Every entity in the requirements maps to a schema object, and every relationship is declared as a foreign key, a reference, or an explicit documented decision to denormalize with its consistency cost stated.
3. **AR-143 — Typed facts, typed columns.** Dates, money, enums, and statuses use typed columns, never strings. Money is integer minor units or a decimal type, never float.
4. **AR-144 — One writable home per fact.** The same fact has exactly one writable home; copies are read models with a named synchronization mechanism and a stated staleness bound.
5. **AR-145 — Index from named queries.** Every query used by a main screen is backed by an index, proven with the database's explain-plan tool, not assumed.
6. **AR-146 — Embed vs reference is decided per relationship.** Embed what is read together and owned together; reference what is shared or independently growing. The decision is recorded for each relationship, not defaulted for the whole store.
7. **AR-147 — One owner per store.** Cross-service data is owned by one service; other services hold references or replicated read models, never shared write access to another service's tables.
8. **AR-148 — Migrations only.** Schema evolution happens only through versioned migrations; manual edits to a live schema are forbidden.
9. **AR-149 — Tenant key from the first migration.** In any multitenant design, tenant-owned tables carry the tenant key from the first migration; retrofitting it later is treated as a redesign, not a migration.
10. **AR-150 — Constraints live in the database.** Integrity invariants (non-null, uniqueness, referential integrity, value ranges) are enforced by database constraints, not by application code alone.
11. **AR-151 — Denormalization is a documented decision.** Every denormalized field names its source of truth and the path that keeps it current; an undocumented copy is a defect.
12. **AR-152 — Every migration has a way back.** Each migration is reversible, or ships with a documented forward-fix procedure; an irreversible migration with neither is not merged.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-071 — Stringly-typed facts.** Banned: storing dates, money, enums, or statuses as free-text strings. Defeats: DET-CODE-025. Instead: an enum or lookup type with a check constraint, and money as integer minor units. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-072 — Two writable homes for one fact.** Banned: the same fact stored in two places, both writable, updated by different code. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Instead: one owning table; the second consumer gets a read model with a named sync mechanism. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-073 — Shared write access across services.** Banned: one service writing directly into another service's tables. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Instead: call the owning service's API, consume its events, or build a replicated read model. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-074 — Unbounded, unindexed main-screen query.** Banned: a query behind a main screen with no index support and no row limit. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: an index on the sort/filter columns, cursor pagination, and explain-plan evidence attached to the change. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-071 — Migration build check.** Verifies: AR-142, AR-148. Check: automated — CI applies all migrations to an empty database and diffs the resulting schema against the declared model. Pass: migrations apply cleanly and the diff is empty. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-072 — Explain-plan evidence.** Verifies: AR-145. Check: automated — the test harness runs EXPLAIN for each named main-screen query against a production-shaped dataset. Pass: every query uses its intended index; no sequential scan over a large table. Fail: block the schema change until the index exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-073 — Duplicate-fact audit.** Verifies: AR-144, AR-151. Check: manual — pick three core facts and trace each to its single writable home, naming the sync mechanism for every copy found. Pass: 3 of 3 facts have exactly one writable home. Fail: block release until the duplicate is demoted to a read model. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-074 — Tenant-key schema check (citation).** Verifies: AR-149. Check: automated — this requirement is verified by the canonical tenant-key schema check, G-AR-092 in multitenancy-saas (every tenant-owned table carries a non-null tenant key with a leading index); run that gate for the full procedure and pass criteria. Single-tenant projects record the exemption in ARCHITECTURE.md. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Access patterns first, nouns last.
- Every fact has one writable home.
- Typed facts get typed columns; money is never float.
- Indexes are proven with explain plans, not assumed.
- Evolution happens only through migrations.

## Checklist

- [ ] The access-pattern list exists and every main screen and job is on it (AR-141).
- [ ] Every requirement entity maps to a schema object; every relationship is declared (AR-142).
- [ ] No stringly-typed dates, money, enums, or statuses; money is integer minor units or decimal (AR-143).
- [ ] Duplicate-fact audit passed: 3 of 3 core facts traced to one writable home (G-AR-073).
- [ ] Explain-plan evidence attached for every named main-screen query (G-AR-072).
- [ ] Tenant-owned tables carry the tenant key from the first migration, or the single-tenant exemption is recorded (AR-149).
- [ ] Every migration is reversible or carries a forward-fix procedure (AR-152).

---

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/domain-driven-design/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# domain-driven-design

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Eric Evans, *Domain-Driven Design Reference* (definitions of bounded context, aggregate, ubiquitous language) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/ ; Pattern context for how DDD boundaries interact with data ownership and sagas — https://microservices.io/
- **Depends on:** requirements-writing, system-design
- **Feeds into:** data-architecture, api-architecture, schema-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a domain is complex enough that its language and consistency rules drive the design: finding bounded contexts, drawing aggregates around invariants, building the ubiquitous language, or mapping how contexts integrate.
- **Do NOT use when:** the area is plain CRUD over one table with no invariants worth the name — model it as a simple CRUD module (AR-228) and spend the effort elsewhere. Do not use this skill as a naming ceremony for a design already fixed; the language work comes first or not at all.

## Rules

1. **AR-221 — Language first.** The ubiquitous language is built from domain conversations and the requirements before tactical modeling starts; one term has one meaning inside a context.
2. **AR-222 — Contexts are recorded.** Every bounded context has a name, a one-paragraph responsibility, its context-map relationships, and an owning module or service, recorded in ARCHITECTURE.md. A context that exists only in a slide is not a context.
3. **AR-223 — Boundaries follow language shifts.** Where the same word changes meaning (an "order" in sales is not an "order" in fulfillment), that shift marks a context boundary.
4. **AR-224 — Aggregates follow invariants.** If two objects must be consistent in the same transaction, they belong to one aggregate; if not, they reference each other by identity and accept eventual consistency.
5. **AR-225 — References by identity across aggregates.** Code never reaches through one aggregate's object graph into another's internals; cross-aggregate references are by ID.
6. **AR-226 — Declared cross-context mechanisms only.** Contexts communicate through the mechanism the context map declares (API, events, anti-corruption layer). Direct reads of another context's tables are forbidden.
7. **AR-227 — The glossary is testable.** Type, field, and endpoint names inside a context use its glossary terms verbatim; a synonym introduced in code is a defect.
8. **AR-228 — Honest CRUD.** An area that is CRUD over one table is modeled and named as a simple CRUD module, not dressed in tactical DDD vocabulary it does not use.
9. **AR-229 — Inferred terms are flagged.** When no domain expert is available, the glossary is derived from the requirements and fact sheet, and every inferred term is marked UNVERIFIED until a domain source confirms it.
10. **AR-230 — Domain events mark real state changes.** Events crossing a context boundary are named from the domain language for state changes that actually happened (see event-driven), not for technical row mutations.
11. **AR-231 — Invariants are enforced in one transaction.** For every named invariant, one aggregate enforces it atomically; an invariant checked in one transaction and applied in another is unenforced.
12. **AR-232 — Anti-corruption layer at hostile boundaries.** Integration with a legacy or external model goes through an anti-corruption layer that translates it into this context's language; foreign terms never leak inward.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-111 — Reading another context's tables.** Banned: one bounded context querying another context's database tables directly. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Instead: consume the sales context's published API or events, through an anti-corruption layer if its model is foreign. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-112 — Synonym drift.** Banned: introducing a code name that differs from the glossary term for the same concept. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: rename the code to the glossary term — `customer` everywhere in this context — and treat the rename as a defect fix, not a refactor. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-113 — Tactical theater.** Banned: wrapping plain CRUD in aggregates, repositories, and domain services that add no invariant or language value. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Instead: model it as an honest CRUD module and reserve tactical patterns for contexts with real invariants. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-114 — Invariant split across transactions.** Banned: checking a consistency invariant in one transaction and applying the change in another. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: enforce the invariant inside the aggregate's transaction — the seat inventory aggregate decrements and rejects atomically. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-111 — Glossary cross-check.** Verifies: AR-227. Check: manual — sample type and field names from the codebase and API schemas and match each against the context glossaries. Pass: every sampled name is a glossary term used verbatim. Fail: warn; each synonym found is filed as a defect. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-112 — Context dependency check.** Verifies: AR-226. Check: automated — CI module-dependency rules fail the build when one context imports another context's internals or connects to its tables. Pass: the check exits 0. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-113 — Invariant trace.** Verifies: AR-224, AR-231. Check: manual — pick one named invariant and find the aggregate that enforces it, in a single transaction, in code. Pass: the enforcing aggregate and transaction are identified. Fail: block release until the invariant has an owner. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-114 — Context record completeness.** Verifies: AR-222. Check: automated — a script over ARCHITECTURE.md asserts every context section carries a name, responsibility paragraph, context-map relationships, and an owning module. Pass: all four fields present for every context. Fail: block merge of the architecture change. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- One term, one meaning, per context.
- A word changing meaning marks a boundary.
- Aggregates follow invariants, not diagrams.
- Contexts talk through the map's declared mechanisms only.
- Plain CRUD is modeled as plain CRUD.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every bounded context is recorded with name, responsibility, relationships, and owner (AR-222).
- [ ] The glossary lives in the repo and inferred terms are marked UNVERIFIED (AR-229).
- [ ] Glossary cross-check passed on sampled code and schema names (G-AR-111).
- [ ] Context dependency check exits 0 in CI (G-AR-112).
- [ ] One named invariant was traced to the aggregate enforcing it in a single transaction (G-AR-113).
- [ ] Cross-context integrations use the context map's declared mechanisms, with an ACL where the model is foreign (AR-226, AR-232).
- [ ] CRUD-only areas are named and modeled as CRUD modules (AR-228).

---

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/event-driven/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# event-driven

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Fowler, "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?" — https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html ; AsyncAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.1.0 ; CloudEvents (CNCF envelope attributes) — http://cloudevents.io/ ; Zalando event guidelines (events as interface, compatibility, no sensitive personal data) — https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/
- **Depends on:** architecture-patterns, api-architecture, adr-writing
- **Feeds into:** queues-jobs, notifications, realtime

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** components communicate through events or messages: introducing a broker or stream, defining an event type, making consumers reliable, or auditing an existing event flow for coupling and correctness.
- **Do NOT use when:** a synchronous call is the honest shape of the interaction (the caller needs the answer to proceed) — use api-architecture and make the call. Do not use this skill to justify a broker for a system with no independent consumers; that is the decorative-infrastructure failure in architecture-patterns.

## Rules

1. **AR-201 — Name the pattern first.** Choose and record which pattern applies — event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing, or CQRS — before building; the four have different consistency and coupling consequences and are not interchangeable.
2. **AR-202 — Events are facts.** Events are named in the past tense (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentFailed`) and state something that already happened; an event is never a command a producer secretly depends on one specific consumer executing.
3. **AR-203 — Every event is a contract.** Each event type has an entry in the AsyncAPI document, a versioned payload schema, a named owner, and a list of known consumers.
4. **AR-204 — CloudEvents envelope.** Every event carries the standard envelope attributes — `specversion`, `id`, `source`, `type` — so events stay routable and deduplicatable across brokers and vendors.
5. **AR-205 — Publication is atomic.** Events are published atomically with the business write (transactional outbox or an event store). Writing to the database and then publishing as a separate step is a defect.
6. **AR-206 — Consumers are idempotent.** A consumer deduplicates on event `id` and `source` and produces the same effect whether an event arrives once or five times.
7. **AR-207 — Ordering scope is stated.** Each stream declares its ordering scope (per aggregate or per key, via partitioning), and consumers tolerate out-of-order delivery within that scope.
8. **AR-208 — Poison messages go to a dead-letter queue.** After bounded retries, a failing message lands in a DLQ with an alert. Infinite retry and silent dropping are both forbidden.
9. **AR-209 — Minimum payload.** Payloads carry only the data the chosen pattern requires. Full entity snapshots under event-carried state transfer require an explicit ADR, and events never carry sensitive personal data beyond need.
10. **AR-210 — A replay procedure exists.** Every stream documents how a consumer rebuilds state or reprocesses from a chosen point, and the procedure is exercised before it is needed in an incident.
11. **AR-211 — Schema evolution is compatibility-checked.** New payload schema versions are checked against the previous version under the compatibility rules (additive changes safe; removals and retypes breaking) before deployment.
12. **AR-212 — Consumers fail independently.** A producer keeps working while any consumer is down, and when the consumer returns, the backlog drains with no duplicate effects applied.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-101 — A command in event's clothing.** Banned: naming or using an event as an imperative command that one named consumer is expected to execute. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Instead: publish the fact (`UserRegistered`) and let the email service decide, as a known consumer, to send the email. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-102 — Dual-write publication.** Banned: writing to the database and publishing the event as two uncoordinated steps. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and let a relay publish from the outbox. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-103 — Swallowed poison messages.** Banned: a consumer catching all exceptions, acknowledging the message, and moving on with no record. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: bounded retries, then the dead-letter queue with an alert and the payload preserved for inspection. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-104 — Unversioned payload changed in place.** Banned: changing a published event's payload shape without a new schema version and compatibility check. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: add the new field, keep the old one through the deprecation window, and bump the schema version with a compatibility check in CI. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-101 — Contract and compatibility check.** Verifies: AR-203, AR-211. Check: automated — the AsyncAPI document validates in CI, and each new payload schema is compatibility-checked against its previous version. Pass: validation exits 0 and no unapproved breaking schema change. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-102 — Replay and duplicate-delivery test.** Verifies: AR-206, AR-210. Check: automated — recorded events are replayed against consumers in CI, with each event delivered twice. Pass: final state equals the single-delivery state; no duplicate effects. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-103 — Consumer-outage test.** Verifies: AR-212. Check: mechanized manual — in staging, disable one consumer, run normal producer traffic, then restore the consumer. Pass: producers are unaffected while it is down, and the backlog drains afterward with no duplicates applied. Fail: block release until the consumer is decoupled. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-104 — Outbox path check.** Verifies: AR-205. Check: automated — search the codebase for direct broker-publish calls outside the outbox relay module. Pass: none found; all publication flows through the outbox. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Name the pattern before building anything.
- Events are facts in the past tense, never commands.
- Publish atomically: outbox or event store, never dual write.
- Consumers deduplicate, tolerate disorder, and dead-letter poison.
- A consumer down must never take the producer with it.

## Checklist

- [ ] The pattern (notification, state transfer, event sourcing, CQRS) is named and recorded (AR-201).
- [ ] Every event type has an AsyncAPI entry, a versioned schema, an owner, and known consumers (AR-203).
- [ ] Every event carries the CloudEvents envelope attributes (AR-204).
- [ ] Outbox path check passes: no direct broker publishes outside the relay (G-AR-104).
- [ ] Replay test passes with duplicate delivery producing no duplicate effects (G-AR-102).
- [ ] Consumer-outage test passed in staging within the current release cycle (G-AR-103).
- [ ] Every stream has a DLQ with an alert and a documented replay procedure (AR-208, AR-210).

# multitenancy-saas

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microsoft Learn, multitenancy and Azure SQL Database (tenancy models, row-level security, noisy neighbor) — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/service/sql-database ; Microsoft Learn, multitenancy tenancy models for Cosmos DB — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/multi-tenancy-vector-search
- **Depends on:** system-design, data-architecture, backend-auth
- **Feeds into:** tenant-isolation, schema-design, subscriptions

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product serves more than one customer organization or consumer from one deployment and the isolation model must be chosen, implemented, or audited — tenancy model selection, tenant context handling, provisioning, per-tenant operations.
- **Do NOT use when:** the product is single-tenant by design — say so in ARCHITECTURE.md and stop. Do not use this skill for the database-level implementation of row-level security itself; that is tenant-isolation and schema-design, working from the model chosen here. Data-level isolation enforcement and its review — tenant scoping across tables, queries, jobs, and cache keys — belongs to tenant-isolation (D5); this skill owns only the model-level choice and audit.

## Rules

1. **AR-181 — Tenant is defined first.** State what a tenant is (customer organization, individual consumer, or sub-unit) before choosing any model; the definition drives isolation, billing, and data-sovereignty requirements.
2. **AR-182 — Model per layer, named from the catalog.** Choose per layer from the named models — shared schema with tenant key (pool), schema/database per tenant (silo), or hybrid (bridge) — and record the choice in an ADR citing the isolation, compliance, and cost trade-offs.
3. **AR-183 — Context is established at the edge.** Tenant context is resolved once, at the request boundary, from the authenticated principal or the subdomain, and propagated. Code never accepts a tenant ID from an unauthenticated request body.
4. **AR-184 — Every path is scoped.** Every query path — API, admin, reporting, export, and background jobs — is scoped by tenant. An unscoped path is a blocker defect.
5. **AR-185 — Isolation is platform-enforced.** Scoping is applied automatically (ORM filter, row-level security, middleware), never by each developer remembering a filter per query.
6. **AR-186 — Tenant key on every tenant-owned table.** The key is non-null, present from the first migration, and leads the index used by tenant-scoped queries.
7. **AR-187 — Per-tenant operations are designed.** Backup and restore granularity, data export, and tenant deletion (including legal erasure) are specified for the chosen model before the first tenant onboards.
8. **AR-188 — Provisioning is automated.** New tenants are created by an automated, tested procedure. Manual database edits are not a provisioning path.
9. **AR-189 — Noisy-neighbor controls are part of the model.** Per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and per-tenant usage observability ship with the design, not after the first incident.
10. **AR-190 — Hybrid placements are enumerated.** In a bridge model, a tenant catalog records which tenant lives in which store; routing reads the catalog, never a hardcoded list in code.
11. **AR-191 — Async work carries tenant context.** Background jobs and event consumers receive and propagate tenant context; work that arrives without it fails closed rather than running unscoped.
12. **AR-192 — Isolation is tested, not assumed.** The cross-tenant test suite is part of the design deliverable, and it runs in CI from the first tenant onward.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-091 — Tenant ID from the request body.** Banned: resolving the tenant from a client-supplied value in an unauthenticated request. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Instead: resolve the tenant from the authenticated principal (or the subdomain, verified against the session) at the edge and ignore body-supplied tenant values entirely. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-092 — Isolation by developer memory.** Banned: tenant scoping that depends on each query's author remembering to add the filter. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: enforce scoping in the platform layer — row-level security or an ORM-level automatic filter — so an unscoped query returns nothing rather than everything. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-093 — Manual provisioning.** Banned: creating a tenant by hand-editing the production database. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Instead: a scripted, tested provisioning procedure that creates the tenant atomically and is exercised in staging on every release. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-094 — Unbounded shared tenants.** Banned: shared compute and storage with no per-tenant rate limit or quota. Defeats: DET-INF-023. Instead: per-tenant rate limits and quotas at the edge and in the job queue, with per-tenant usage visible on a dashboard. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-091 — Cross-tenant test suite.** Verifies: AR-184, AR-192. Check: automated — authenticate as tenant A and attempt reads, writes, and exports against tenant B's known resource IDs through every interface class (API, export, report, job trigger). Pass: every attempt returns 403 or 404 and writes nothing. Fail: block release; a single cross-tenant success is a P0 defect. Recorded in: progress.md. Execution: this gate is specified here and executed by D8 (QA & Testing) in its test harness, with auth fixtures owned by D4/D7 and tenant data fixtures owned by D5.
- **G-AR-092 — Tenant-key schema check.** Verifies: AR-186. Check: automated — script asserts every table flagged tenant-owned has a non-null tenant key column and an index leading with it. Pass: zero violations. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md. Execution: this gate is specified here (canonical — data-architecture G-AR-074 cites it) and executed by D8 (QA & Testing), with schema fixtures owned by D5.
- **G-AR-093 — Provisioning drill.** Verifies: AR-188. Check: automated — run the provisioning procedure in staging, then verify the new tenant can sign in, sees an empty workspace, and appears in the tenant catalog. Pass: tenant fully created with no manual step. Fail: block the release that changed provisioning. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-094 — Noisy-neighbor review.** Verifies: AR-189. Check: manual — confirm per-tenant rate limits and quotas are configured and per-tenant usage metrics are visible on an operations dashboard. Pass: limits configured and metrics visible for every tenant. Fail: warn; schedule the fix before onboarding the next tenant. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Define the tenant before choosing the model.
- Context comes from the edge, never from the body.
- Every path is scoped — admin, exports, and jobs included.
- Isolation is enforced by the platform, not by memory.
- Provisioning is a procedure, not a person with SQL access.

## Checklist

- [ ] The tenant definition is written down and the per-layer model is chosen in an ADR (AR-181, AR-182).
- [ ] Tenant context is resolved once at the edge from the authenticated principal or subdomain (AR-183).
- [ ] Cross-tenant test suite passes: every cross-tenant attempt returns 403/404 and writes nothing (G-AR-091).
- [ ] Tenant-key schema check passes on every tenant-owned table (G-AR-092).
- [ ] Backup/restore granularity, export, and tenant deletion are specified for the model (AR-187).
- [ ] Provisioning drill passes in staging with no manual step (G-AR-093).
- [ ] Per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and usage metrics are in place (AR-189).
